docs.title: API verification
docs.text: Connect IQ's API differs by API level and by device. A method can exist in the SDK but be missing from a given watch. Code that guesses an API name or signature may compile and then fail on the device. The project rule is: never guess an API. Any call not already used in the codebase is confirmed first.

docs.title: tools/ciq_api.py
docs.text:
The SDK ships its full API reference as HTML. A small standard-library script reads it locally, with no network access:

$ python3 tools/ciq_api.py Graphics.Dc setAntiAlias
Toybox.Graphics.Dc.setAntiAlias(enabled as Lang.Boolean) as Void
  Enable anti-aliased drawing for primitives This method is not supported for a BufferedBitmap that has a palette.
  Since: API Level 3.2.0
  fēnix® 8 Solar 47mm: SUPPORTED

It:

  1. Finds the SDK the SDK Manager has selected (current-sdk.cfg) or $CIQ_SDK.
  2. Opens doc/Toybox/<Module>/<Class>.html and finds the member's detail block by its anchor id.
  3. Strips the HTML and extracts the signature, the start of the description and Since: API Level.
  4. Checks the Supported Devices list, if the method has one, for the target device.

The exit codes make it usable in scripts:

Exit Meaning 0 Supported, or no device list (available on every device at that API level) 1 Page or member not found 2 Usage error 3 The method has a device list and the target isn't in it. Don't use it.

docs.title: APIs confirmed this way
docs.text:
The spec marked several API names "(check)" because they were written from memory. Among those confirmed before use:

API Result How it is used Dc.setAntiAlias API 3.2.0, device listed Guarded with dc has :setAntiAlias anyway Dc.fillPolygon the docs give a 64-point limit Largest polygon is the 12-point duck body Dc.fillCircle, Dc.drawLine available Dot matrix, duck, wing Complications types BODY_BATTERY, SUNRISE, SUNSET, HEART_RATE available All four live fields ActivityMonitor.Info.distance unit is centimetres Converted to tenths of km or mi System.Stats.solarIntensity null without solar, negative when not charging Shown as 0% Graphics.getVectorFont :size not documented Measured: it is the full line height, not the em

The last row shows what the docs can't answer. The meaning of :size was determined in the simulator against the TTF's hhea metrics, and the result is recorded next to the constant that depends on it.

docs.title: Permissions follow from the APIs
docs.text: Because each API was checked, the manifest requests only what the code uses: ComplicationSubscriber, SensorHistory and UserProfile. Positioning was avoided by reading sunrise and sunset from complications rather than computing them from a location.

docs.title: build.sh
docs.text:
./build.sh          # debug build: bin/WatchFace.prg (memory logging, Demo module)
./build.sh run      # debug build, then load into a running simulator
./build.sh release  # release build (-r): bin/WatchFace-release.prg, debug code stripped
  • The signing key never appears in the repository. Its path is read from a git-ignored .env (GARMIN_DEV_KEY), and .gitignore also excludes *.der, *.pem and developer_key* as a second line of defence.
  • The SDK is located automatically from the SDK Manager's current-sdk.cfg, or from $CIQ_SDK, so the script works for whichever SDK version is selected.
  • Warnings are on (-w), and the project rule is that a build with any warning isn't done.
  • run also pushes the settings JSON to the simulator (-a bin/WatchFace-settings.json:GARMIN/Settings/…), so its settings editor can find the face's settings.
  • set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first failure.

docs.title: Debug and release builds from one source
docs.text:
Monkey C supports build annotations. A function or module marked (:debug) is compiled only into debug builds, and one marked (:release) only into release builds (monkeyc -r). The face uses pairs of implementations with the same signature:

(:debug)
private function logMemory(tag as String) as Void {
    var stats = System.getSystemStats();
    System.println("mem[" + tag + "] used=" + stats.usedMemory + " free=" + stats.freeMemory + " total=" + stats.totalMemory);
}

(:release)
private function logMemory(tag as String) as Void {
}
Hook Debug build Release build logMemory(tag) prints heap usage after layout and every minute empty logGraph() prints bar count, newest sample, resting HR, all 24 bpm values empty applyDemo(dc) overrides live data with a mockup state empty demoActive() Demo.STATE != 0 false demoMinute(m) Demo.TIME if set, else the real minute the real minute module Demo mockup values, about 1.5 KB not compiled

The call sites stay the same in both builds, and the release binary contains no demo data, logging strings or debug branches.

docs.title: Demo mode
docs.text:
source/Demo.mc turns the simulator into a test fixture:

const STATE = 0;    // 0 = live data, 1 = normal, 2 = targets met, 3 = running low
const TIME = -1;    // minutes after midnight to show, or -1 for the clock
  • STATE 1–3 feeds the exact values read off the three design mockups (battery, solar, Body Battery, calories, steps, distance, heart rate, resting heart rate and all 24 graph bars) through the real formatting, layout and colour-rule code. The rendering can then be compared against the mockups, and every colour rule can be triggered on demand.
  • TIME pins the displayed hours and minutes, for example 12 * 60 + 25 so that two 2s appear for the rubber duck.
  • Both must be committed as 0 and -1. The local packaging script refuses to build a store package when STATE ≠ 0, so a demo build can't be shipped by accident.

docs.title: Release and packaging
docs.text:
1. ./build.sh release builds a release .prg to check that it compiles without the debug code.
  2. A local, git-ignored packaging script exports the signed .iq store package (monkeyc -e -r -w). It first checks that Demo.STATE is 0.
  3. The store version is tagged in git (v1.0.0) on the commit whose source matches the uploaded package.

docs.title: Simulator workflow
docs.text:
connectiq &              # start the simulator once
./build.sh run           # build and load; repeat after each change

The project's build skill also documents:

  • forcing a setting (temporarily returning a fixed value from Settings.timeFont()) to measure the worst-case memory or take a screenshot of a given style, then restoring the file
  • measuring a baseline by building an earlier commit in a throwaway git worktree

Low-power behaviour is tested with the simulator's Always-On display mode (see Low power).

docs.title: Design preview renderer
docs.text:
Changing a watch face's typography is expensive to get wrong: each attempt costs a Monkey C port, a build and a simulator check, and the result may still not fit. For the time-font and rubber-duck features, candidates were judged before any Monkey C existed, with a Python renderer that shows them as they would appear on the watch.

Source: tools/preview/ (about 1,100 lines of Python with Pillow and NumPy).

docs.title: What "pixel-accurate" means here
docs.text:
Watch behaviour How the renderer reproduces it 260 × 260 px screen Renders at 260 px onto a real simulator screenshot of the face, so the candidate is seen in context. 64 colours Every output pixel is snapped to the nearest of 0x00/0x55/0xAA/0xFF per channel (snap()). Anti-aliased bitmap fonts Coverage blended, then snapped. Hard-edged fonts and shapes Binary coverage, no blending. fillCircle / fillPolygon with setAntiAlias Shapes painted at 8× supersampling and downsampled, then snapped. Exact placement The current time is erased from the screenshot. The week number and seconds are cut out and re-placed at the position the new style would produce. 
LEVELS = np.array([0, 85, 170, 255])

def snap(rgb):
    return LEVELS[np.abs(rgb[..., None] - LEVELS).argmin(-1)]

docs.title: Fitting over every minute
docs.text:
Each candidate is fitted before it is shown: it is scaled to the largest size whose digits stay within 47 px and whose widest time over all 1,440 minutes stays within 127 px. Testing only 10:08 would miss the times that break the layout. That depends on each font's digit widths: a font with a wide 0 fails at 00:00, and one with a wide 2 at 22:22.

def all_times():
    return [f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}" for h in range(24) for m in range(60)]

The fitted size and the margin to the side panel are reported for each option, and those numbers went straight into make_fonts.py (Saira at 41 px digits). A later round used the same fitting to make Handwritten taller: Kalam narrowed to 84 % reaches 44 px digits within the same 127 px.

docs.title: Scripts
docs.text: Script Produces render.py Shared library: TTF fitting, 7-segment and dot-matrix drawing, MIP snapping, compositing onto the screenshot. build.py Round 1: every candidate font fitted to the time's box, four sample times each plus its widest time, a memory estimate, a contact sheet. ghost.py Dot-matrix variants with fractional pitch and supersampled round dots. duck.py Rubber-duck designs in each of the five fonts, from shape functions in unit coordinates. page.py, duck_page.py Self-contained HTML comparison pages: one card per option with an ID, the full face, a time switcher, and facts such as size compared with today, memory or "drawn in code", and licence.

docs.title: From preview to production
docs.text:
The workflow, recorded as a project skill so it can be repeated:

  1. Fit, don't redesign. Every option must fit the box the current element uses.
  2. Render honestly. Use the real pixel size, the 64-colour palette, and anti-aliasing only where the watch would use it.
  3. Look before publishing. Make a contact sheet, and drop options that are broken or illegible.
  4. Publish a comparison page and ask for feedback by option ID.
  5. Iterate on the picks.
  6. Port exactly. The chosen geometry stays in the scripts. duck.py's tall_neck() and TimeDisplay.buildDuck() use the same unit coordinates, so the watch reproduces what was approved.

docs.title: Documentation figures
docs.text: The figures on this site use the same "derive it from the source" approach. tools/docs/make_assets.py parses the constant arrays in Icons.mc and TimeDisplay.mc and the spec constants in the view, and renders the icon grids, the 7-segment and dot-matrix glyph sheets, the layout map and the font atlases. If an icon changes in code, running the script updates the docs.
